source.authority: The supplied article is authoritative for source-grounded claims.
source.provenance_note: Source line ranges refer to the line markers shown in the supplied extracted article; explanatory synthesis is distinguished from source claims.

overview: A relationship-rich semantic graph of network routing: path selection, routing algorithms, delivery schemes, protocol families, metrics, multi-agent policies, congestion, hardware/software implementation, history, and route analytics.

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.description: Selecting paths for traffic through a network or across interconnected networks; higher-level path decisions are distinct from per-hop packet forwarding.

nodes.label: Packet switching
nodes.description: Traffic is carried as packets through intermediate nodes.

nodes.label: Packet forwarding
nodes.description: Moves a received packet from an incoming interface to an outgoing interface; it implements the next-hop action selected by routing.

nodes.label: Route
nodes.description: A destination paired with reachability/path information or attributes.

nodes.label: Routing table
nodes.description: Records routes to network destinations and supports forwarding decisions.

nodes.label: Forwarding information base (FIB)
nodes.description: Forwarding-optimized table built from control-plane routing information and consulted by the forwarding plane.

nodes.label: Control plane
nodes.description: Computes and distributes route information and derives the FIB.

nodes.label: Forwarding plane
nodes.description: Examines packet headers, matches destinations against the FIB, and forwards packets to outgoing interfaces.

nodes.label: Router
nodes.description: Intermediate network node that routes IP packets between networks.

nodes.label: Gateway
nodes.description: Interconnects different networks; historically used as a term for router-like devices.

nodes.label: Switch
nodes.description: Forwards traffic within networks; Layer-3 switches can also interconnect subnets using routing.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.description: May be an intermediate forwarding node and may impose filtering/security policy.

nodes.label: Network node
nodes.description: A device or logical point participating in a network and routing/forwarding.

nodes.label: Network interface
nodes.description: Physical or logical attachment through which packets enter or leave a network device.

nodes.label: Destination address
nodes.description: Address used to identify the target network or endpoint; structured IP prefixes enable aggregate routes.

nodes.label: IP address
nodes.description: Network-layer address used by IP routing decisions.

nodes.label: Network prefix
nodes.description: Structured portion of an address that identifies a network/subnet and permits aggregate route entries.

nodes.label: Subnet
nodes.description: Logical network with a unique network prefix; routers connect subnets.

nodes.label: Next hop
nodes.description: The adjacent router/interface or node to which a packet is sent toward its destination.

nodes.label: Network topology
nodes.description: Graph of nodes and connections; dynamic topology changes make manual routes impractical at scale.

nodes.label: Network link
nodes.description: Connection between nodes; algorithms may assign it a cost.

nodes.label: Link cost
nodes.description: Numeric cost assigned to a link and accumulated across a path by distance-vector or shortest-path algorithms.

nodes.label: Path
nodes.description: Sequence of links/nodes or routing domains that traffic traverses toward a destination.

nodes.label: Routing metric
nodes.description: Protocol-specific measure used to compare routes; may reflect bandwidth, delay, hops, cost, load, MTU, reliability, or communication cost.

nodes.label: Bandwidth
nodes.description: Available or rated transmission capacity; one possible path-selection metric.

nodes.label: Latency
nodes.description: Delay experienced along a path; can be optimized for interactive requests but may conflict with policy/cost objectives.

nodes.label: Hop count
nodes.description: Number of routing hops on a path; one possible metric.

nodes.label: Reliability
nodes.description: A possible route-selection metric describing link/path reliability.

nodes.label: Maximum transmission unit (MTU)
nodes.description: Maximum packet size supported by a path/interface; listed as a possible routing metric in the source.

nodes.label: Static routing
nodes.description: Manually configured routes; useful in small or stable networks and can provide host-specific control.

nodes.label: Dynamic routing
nodes.description: Automatically updates route tables using routing-protocol information as topology changes.

nodes.label: Distance-vector routing
nodes.description: Routers share destination reachability and costs with neighbors; the Bellman–Ford approach is used in the source description.

nodes.label: Bellman–Ford algorithm
nodes.description: Computes least-cost paths through iterative distance/cost updates; underlies distance-vector routing as described in the article.

nodes.label: Link-state routing
nodes.description: Nodes disseminate link-state information, build topology maps, and independently calculate shortest paths.

nodes.label: Dijkstra algorithm
nodes.description: Shortest-path algorithm used on a link-state topology map to compute least-cost paths from a root node.

nodes.label: Optimized Link State Routing (OLSR)
nodes.description: Proactive link-state protocol for mobile ad hoc networks using Hello and Topology Control messages and multipoint relays.

nodes.label: Hello messages
nodes.description: OLSR messages used to discover one-hop and two-hop neighborhood information.

nodes.label: Topology Control (TC) messages
nodes.description: OLSR messages used to disseminate link-state/topology information.

nodes.label: Multipoint relays (MPRs)
nodes.description: Selected OLSR nodes that help disseminate topology information efficiently.

nodes.label: Path-vector routing
nodes.description: Inter-domain routing approach where speakers advertise destination reachability together with path/domain descriptions.

nodes.label: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)
nodes.description: Inter-domain routing protocol used to select AS-level paths between autonomous systems.

nodes.label: Autonomous system (AS)
nodes.description: Network domain administered as a routing unit; Internet inter-domain paths traverse ASs.

nodes.label: Speaker node
nodes.description: Node representing an AS for exchanging path-vector reachability with neighboring AS speakers.

nodes.label: AS path
nodes.description: Sequence of routing domains traversed by reachability information; a path-vector attribute.

nodes.label: Intra-domain routing
nodes.description: Routing within a single autonomous system; distance-vector and link-state protocols are described as intra-domain.

nodes.label: Inter-domain routing
nodes.description: Routing between autonomous systems; path-vector routing is used for this scale.

nodes.label: Routing Information Protocol (RIP)
nodes.description: Example of a dynamic routing protocol based on distance-vector routing.

nodes.label: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
nodes.description: Example of a dynamic routing protocol using link-state ideas.

nodes.label: Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol (EIGRP)
nodes.description: Example dynamic routing protocol listed in the source.

nodes.label: Unicast
nodes.description: One-to-one delivery to a specific receiver.

nodes.label: Broadcast
nodes.description: One-to-all delivery within the applicable broadcast scope, with network replication as needed.

nodes.label: Multicast
nodes.description: Delivery to a defined interested group rather than all nodes.

nodes.label: Anycast
nodes.description: One-of-many delivery to one member of a group sharing an address, typically selected by routing cost/distance.

nodes.label: Longest-prefix match
nodes.description: Among matching entries, a longer prefix is more specific and is preferred.

nodes.label: Administrative distance
nodes.description: External preference value for comparing route sources/protocols in implementations such as Cisco; lower values are preferred.

nodes.label: Route redistribution
nodes.description: Selective sharing of routes between multiple routing protocols running on the same router.

nodes.label: Default route
nodes.description: Route used when no more specific destination route matches; commonly sends non-local traffic to an ISP.

nodes.label: Host-specific route
nodes.description: Route targeting a particular host, used for control, testing, or security.

nodes.label: Equal-cost multipath (ECMP)
nodes.description: Uses multiple alternative paths when route costs are equal.

nodes.label: Multipath routing
nodes.description: Uses multiple available paths rather than a single path.

nodes.label: Centralized routing
nodes.description: A logically centralized controller can optimize forwarding state for network-wide objectives, including in SDN-style systems.

nodes.label: Software-defined networking (SDN)
nodes.description: Architecture allowing logically centralized control over forwarding state.

nodes.label: Next-hop routing
nodes.description: Each node chooses the next hop instead of requiring one device to calculate an entire end-to-end path for every packet.

nodes.label: Deterministic routing
nodes.description: Chooses the same path to a destination until new information changes the preference.

nodes.label: Randomized routing
nodes.description: Uses random choices to avoid congestion hot spots in some packet networks.

nodes.label: Valiant routing paradigm
nodes.description: Routes first to a randomly chosen intermediate destination, then to the true destination.

nodes.label: A* search
nodes.description: A graph-search algorithm that can be used by a planner with sufficient topology knowledge to find a path.

nodes.label: Circuit switching
nodes.description: Historical/high-speed approach that establishes a path for a flow/circuit and reuses it until teardown.

nodes.label: Hot-potato routing
nodes.description: An AS forwards traffic out of its own network at the nearest/lowest internal-cost exit, even if this increases end-to-end latency.

nodes.label: Route analytics
nodes.description: Monitoring route state and network routing posture to detect incorrect routing, flapping, performance degradation, or downtime.

nodes.label: Route flapping
nodes.description: Repeated route changes that can cause performance degradation or downtime.

nodes.label: Black-hole routing/failure
nodes.description: A route/path that causes traffic to be discarded or fail to reach its destination; listed as a related topic.

nodes.label: Congestion
nodes.description: Packet arrival rate exceeds processing/service capacity, requiring queue and drop management.

nodes.label: Tail drop
nodes.description: Drops newly arriving packets once buffer space is exhausted.

nodes.label: Random Early Detection (RED)
nodes.description: Probabilistically drops packets before the buffer is full as a congestion-avoidance mechanism.

nodes.label: Weighted RED (WRED)
nodes.description: RED variant that can drop different traffic types with different aggressiveness.

nodes.label: Quality of Service (QoS)
nodes.description: Traffic classification and scheduling policy that prioritizes packets, especially important for latency-sensitive VoIP.

nodes.label: Traffic classification
nodes.description: Classifies packets to decide processing priority.

nodes.label: Flow completion time
nodes.description: Time required to complete a traffic flow; a global optimization objective in data-center WAN routing.

nodes.label: Network utilization
nodes.description: Degree to which available network capacity is used; a global routing optimization objective.

nodes.label: Business relationship/policy
nodes.description: Inter-AS route selection may reflect peering and commercial relationships rather than latency or path quality.

nodes.label: Road network analogy
nodes.description: A distributed routing example where drivers choose paths to minimize personal travel time.

nodes.label: Braess’s paradox
nodes.description: Adding a road can increase travel time for all users under selfish route selection.

nodes.label: Automated guided vehicle (AGV) routing
nodes.description: A single-agent/reservation model can reserve infrastructure sections to prevent simultaneous conflicting use.

nodes.label: Reservation/context-aware routing
nodes.description: Uses reservations for infrastructure resources to avoid simultaneous conflicts.

nodes.label: Cellular network routing
nodes.description: Path selection can consider latency and packet error rate across links with varying spectral efficiency.

nodes.label: Centralized private WAN optimization
nodes.description: Large private WANs can optimize global performance using centralized routing approaches.

nodes.label: Packet loss
nodes.description: Packets may be dropped under congestion or route failure.

nodes.label: Route convergence
nodes.description: Distributed routers update route information after topology or reachability changes until a consistent usable state emerges.

nodes.label: Network graph
nodes.description: Graph of nodes and links used for shortest-path and global optimization problems.

nodes.label: Routing policy
nodes.description: Rules that constrain or influence route choice beyond simple shortest path or a single metric.

nodes.label: Bridging
nodes.description: Layer-2 forwarding contrasted with IP routing; useful within LANs but less scalable for large structured networks.

nodes.label: Public switched telephone network (PSTN)
nodes.description: Circuit-switched network where precomputed routes and fallback routes are widely used.

nodes.label: Mobile ad hoc network
nodes.description: Infrastructure-light network targeted by OLSR.

nodes.label: Wide area network (WAN)
nodes.description: Network spanning broad geography; routing may optimize QoS and aggregate traffic.

nodes.label: Internet service provider (ISP)
nodes.description: Autonomous system operator exchanging routes and selecting inter-domain and intra-domain paths.

nodes.label: Router-level path
nodes.description: Path through individual routers inside/among networks, distinct from the AS-level path.

nodes.label: AS-level path
nodes.description: Sequence of autonomous systems chosen by BGP.

nodes.label: Path latency inflation
nodes.description: End-to-end latency above an alternative path’s latency due to policy choices such as hot-potato routing.

nodes.label: Traffic engineering
nodes.description: Selecting paths to balance load, improve throughput, or meet latency/completion-time goals.

nodes.label: Link-state flooding
nodes.description: Disseminates topology information across the network so each router can build a topology map.

nodes.label: Topology database
nodes.description: Stores topology information used by link-state algorithms; can preserve more information than the selected-route table.

nodes.label: Distance table
nodes.description: Per-node destinations, estimated total costs, and next hops used by distance-vector algorithms.

nodes.label: Total route cost
nodes.description: Sum of link costs along a path in distance-vector/least-cost routing.

nodes.label: Network/link failure
nodes.description: Node/link failure can invalidate next-hop entries and trigger route updates.

nodes.label: Packet header
nodes.description: Contains destination information used for route lookup; routing generally avoids inspecting payload.

nodes.label: Packet payload
nodes.description: Content generally not inspected for pure IP routing decisions.

nodes.label: Interface queue/buffer
nodes.description: Buffers packets when arrival rates exceed processing or output capacity.

nodes.label: CPU-based forwarding
nodes.description: General-purpose processors can route/forward packets but may be less optimized than specialized hardware.

nodes.label: ASIC-accelerated forwarding
nodes.description: ASICs perform packet processing functions to avoid CPU scheduling overhead for common fast-path operations.

nodes.label: Routing software
nodes.description: Software implementing route calculation, protocols, policy, and control-plane behavior.

nodes.label: Global routing optimization
nodes.description: Network-wide objective such as utilization, deadline delivery, flow completion times, and queue placement.

nodes.label: Path selection
nodes.description: Applies route metrics and policy to select one or more routes from candidates.

nodes.label: Source node
nodes.description: Origin of traffic whose route is selected.

nodes.label: Destination node
nodes.description: Target node or network of traffic.

nodes.label: Intermediate node
nodes.description: Router/gateway/switch or other node forwarding traffic along the path.

nodes.label: Fallback route
nodes.description: Alternative precomputed route used when the preferred route is blocked, as in PSTN examples.

nodes.label: Route advertisement
nodes.description: Sharing reachability/path information with neighbors or peers.

nodes.label: Route source
nodes.description: Origin of route information, such as static configuration or a routing protocol.

nodes.label: Administrative control
nodes.description: Local administrators can configure static/host routes and route policy.

nodes.label: Central routing controller
nodes.description: Logical central control component that can compute network-wide forwarding state.

nodes.label: Multiple routing protocols
nodes.description: A router may run multiple protocols and redistribute selected information between them.

nodes.label: Routing stability
nodes.description: Ability of a routing system to avoid oscillation/instability and converge after changes.

nodes.label: Routing scalability
nodes.description: Ability of routing algorithms to operate with large topology and frequent changes; per-node global knowledge does not scale.

nodes.label: Routing correctness/security
nodes.description: Incorrect routing can degrade performance or cause downtime; route policy and host-specific routes can support control/security.

nodes.label: Donald Davies
nodes.description: Proposed interface computers and contributed to the end-to-end principle and packet-network design.

nodes.label: Wesley Clark
nodes.description: Conceived a similar interface-computer idea for ARPANET in 1967.

nodes.label: Louis Pouzin
nodes.description: Led the CYCLADES network program, an influential datagram-network experiment.

nodes.label: Ginny Travers
nodes.description: Developed the first true IP router at BBN as part of the DARPA effort in 1975–1976.

nodes.label: Mike Brecia
nodes.description: Recognized alongside Ginny Travers and Bob Hinden for early IP routers.

nodes.label: Bob Hinden
nodes.description: Recognized alongside Mike Brecia and Ginny Travers for early IP routers.

nodes.label: William Yeager
nodes.description: Led Stanford’s 1981 multiprotocol router program.

nodes.label: Noel Chiappa
nodes.description: Led MIT’s 1981 multiprotocol router program.

nodes.label: International Network Working Group (INWG)
nodes.description: International group of networking researchers who developed early gateway concepts.

nodes.label: DARPA
nodes.description: Initiated the 1973–1974 internetworking program that contributed to the TCP/IP architecture.

nodes.label: BBN
nodes.description: Organization associated with early IP router development.

nodes.label: ARPANET
nodes.description: Early packet-switched network whose Interface Message Processors had router-like functionality.

nodes.label: NPL network
nodes.description: Donald Davies’s packet network concept and early interface-computer implementation at the UK National Physical Laboratory.

nodes.label: CYCLADES
nodes.description: Datagram-network research program designed by Louis Pouzin during 1972–1973.

nodes.label: Xerox PARC
nodes.description: Produced the PARC Universal Packet system and early operational Xerox routers.

nodes.label: TCP/IP architecture
nodes.description: Protocol architecture created through the DARPA internetworking effort and now widely used.

nodes.label: IEEE Internet Award (2008)
nodes.description: Award recognition for early IP router work by Mike Brecia, Ginny Travers, and Bob Hinden.

nodes.label: Interface Message Processor (IMP)
nodes.description: Early ARPANET interface computer with functionality fundamentally similar to modern routers.

nodes.label: Honeywell 516
nodes.description: Computer platform used for early interface computers and IMPs.

nodes.label: PDP-11
nodes.description: Computer platform used for early IP and multiprotocol routers.

nodes.label: Valiant randomized routing research
nodes.description: Randomized intermediate-destination routing proposed to avoid congestion hot spots.

nodes.label: Path inflation measurement study (2003)
nodes.description: Study reported inflated latency on a substantial share of paths between neighboring ISPs.

nodes.label: Private data-center WAN
nodes.description: Private optical WANs can use centralized routing and global traffic engineering.

nodes.label: RFC 4098
nodes.description: Terminology for benchmarking BGP device convergence in the control plane; cited for BGP router roles.

nodes.label: RFC 3626
nodes.description: Reference associated with OLSR.

nodes.label: Bellman–Ford routing foundation
nodes.description: Algorithmic foundation for distance-vector routing in the article.

nodes.label: Shortest-path algorithm foundation
nodes.description: Dijkstra’s algorithm is named as the link-state shortest-path method.

nodes.label: Survey on Routing Metrics (2007)
nodes.description: Survey cited for the variety of routing metrics.

nodes.label: BGP routing policies in ISP networks
nodes.description: Research on inter-domain route policy and ISP behavior.

nodes.label: Microsoft Global WAN
nodes.description: Example of a large centralized private WAN routing system.

nodes.label: Facebook Express Backbone
nodes.description: Example of a centralized private backbone network.

nodes.label: Google B4
nodes.description: Example of software-defined global WAN routing.

relationships.mechanism: Routing chooses a path or next-hop policy; forwarding executes per-packet transit between interfaces.
relationships.effect: Separates path decision from packet movement.

relationships.mechanism: Selected routes are installed into the routing table.
relationships.effect: Makes selected route information available for forwarding.

formal_models.name: Routing versus forwarding
steps: select route according to protocol and policy
match each packet destination against FIB
conditions: routing is control/path selection; forwarding is per-packet transit

formal_models.name: Distance-vector update
steps: advertise known destination costs to neighbors
compare received estimates with current estimates
install improved cost and next hop

formal_models.name: Link-state shortest path
steps: derive best next hops and routing table
conditions: each router computes its own shortest-path tree

formal_models.name: Path-vector inter-domain route
steps: select an AS-level route under policy
conditions: inter-domain; AS speakers exchange path descriptions

formal_models.name: Route precedence
steps: compare route sources using implementation-specific preference
conditions: metric comparison across protocols is not directly meaningful; administrative distance is implementation-specific

formal_models.name: Message delivery schemes
steps: choose a single receiver, all nodes, an interested group, or one group member
apply address and routing behavior appropriate to scheme
conditions: broadcast scope depends on network/subnet; anycast chooses one member

formal_models.name: Queue congestion and packet drops
steps: compare arrival rate with service rate
apply tail drop, RED, or WRED when queue thresholds/capacity are reached
observe packet loss and possible flow delay
conditions: exact thresholds and policies depend on implementation/configuration

formal_models.name: Hot-potato route choice
steps: choose an AS-level path under BGP policy
hand traffic to neighboring AS at that exit
compare end-to-end latency with alternative paths
conditions: local optimization can conflict with global latency optimization

formal_models.name: Centralized WAN optimization
conditions: logically centralized control; example private data-center WANs

formal_models.name: Distributed convergence after failure
steps: propagate updates until usable alternatives settle
conditions: convergence time and stability depend on protocol/topology

formal_models.name: Metric-based path selection
conditions: best path depends on objective; one metric does not universally optimize all goals

formal_models.name: Randomized intermediate routing
steps: route intermediate traffic to final destination
conditions: described as an approach to reduce congestion hot spots in some packet systems

formal_models.name: Next-hop routing at scale
conditions: no single device needs to calculate or know the complete end-to-end path

formal_models.name: Policy-aware route choice
conditions: commercial policy can choose a path that is not lowest-latency

formal_models.name: Static versus dynamic routing
steps: choose manual configuration for small/stable topology or protocol learning for changing topology
update or maintain routes as conditions change
conditions: the source contrasts manually configured small networks with dynamic large networks

formal_models.name: Multipath and ECMP
conditions: the source says many algorithms use one path, while ECMP/multipath allow alternatives

formal_models.name: AS-level and router-level path selection
steps: select a sequence of ASs using BGP
apply each ISP’s internal path/exit policy
observe end-to-end latency and policy effects
conditions: multiple router-level paths may correspond to one AS-level path

formal_models.name: Route analytics loop
steps: detect incorrect routes, flapping, and downtime signals
adjust routes or policy and observe changes
conditions: source describes monitoring of routing posture and failure/performance issues

source_claims.claim: Routing selects a path; forwarding moves packets between interfaces.
Routing decisions usually rely on routing tables populated manually or with protocol assistance.
Structured IP addresses allow route aggregation and scale better than unstructured bridging in large networks.
Unicast, broadcast, multicast, and anycast represent distinct delivery semantics.
Dynamic routing updates route tables using protocol information and dominates the Internet.
Distance-vector routing uses Bellman–Ford-style iterative neighbor cost exchange.
Link-state routers flood topology information and independently calculate least-cost paths.
OLSR uses Hello, TC, and multipoint relay mechanisms for proactive ad hoc routing.
Path-vector routing advertises path/domain descriptions for inter-domain reachability.
Route selection may consider prefix length, protocol-specific metric, and administrative distance.
Path selection metrics can include bandwidth, delay, hops, cost, load, MTU, reliability, and communication cost.
Congestion may be managed using tail drop, RED, and WRED; QoS prioritizes traffic.
Inter-AS route choices can reflect commercial relationships and hot-potato policies rather than global latency.
Centralized routing can optimize network-wide performance objectives in private WANs.
Incorrect routing and route flapping can cause performance degradation or downtime.
Early router concepts emerged from NPL, ARPANET, CYCLADES, Xerox PARC, and DARPA-related work.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Routing selects a path/next hop; forwarding transits each packet between interfaces.
IP routing uses structured network-layer addresses; bridging is Layer-2 forwarding.
Static routes are configured manually; dynamic routes are learned/updated through protocols.
Distance vector exchanges destination costs with neighbors; link state floods topology information and computes paths locally.
Path vector advertises domain/path descriptions; distance vector advertises destination costs.
Intra-domain routing operates within an AS; inter-domain routing connects ASs.
Unicast targets one receiver; broadcast targets all nodes in scope.
Multicast targets an interested subset; broadcast targets all nodes within scope.
Anycast chooses one of several receivers sharing an address; unicast targets a specific receiver.
The routing table holds route information; the FIB is optimized for forwarding lookups.
Metrics compare routes under a protocol; administrative distance can compare sources in an implementation-specific way.
ECMP uses multiple equal-cost paths instead of only one route.
Hot-potato routing minimizes an ISP’s internal distance to exit, potentially increasing end-to-end latency.
Centralized routing can optimize global state; distributed protocols exchange local route/topology information.
Deterministic routing repeats a preferred path until information changes; randomized routing can choose an intermediate destination.
Tail drop waits for buffer exhaustion; RED begins probabilistic drops earlier.
WRED varies drop behavior by traffic type.
An AS sequence can map to multiple concrete router-level paths.
Metrics quantify path attributes; policies can override a metric-optimal path for business or administrative reasons.
Convergence is the network settling after updates; route selection chooses among candidates at a given moment.

misconceptions.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
misconceptions.correction: Routing selects path/next-hop state; forwarding applies the FIB to individual packets.

misconceptions.misconception: Every router computes the entire end-to-end path for each packet.
misconceptions.correction: Large networks generally use next-hop routing; each node forwards toward the next hop.

misconceptions.misconception: The lowest latency route is always selected.
misconceptions.correction: Metrics and policies vary; BGP decisions may reflect business relationships or hot-potato routing.

misconceptions.misconception: A routing metric can be compared directly across all protocols.
misconceptions.correction: The source says metrics cannot be compared across routes learned from different protocols; implementations may use administrative distance.

misconceptions.misconception: Multicast is the same as broadcast.
misconceptions.correction: Multicast targets an interested subset; broadcast targets all nodes within its scope.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast delivers to every node sharing an address.
misconceptions.correction: Anycast selects one member of the group, usually based on routing distance/cost.

misconceptions.misconception: Static routing is suitable for any rapidly changing large topology.
misconceptions.correction: The source notes manual table construction becomes infeasible for large, rapidly changing networks.

misconceptions.misconception: Link-state routing simply shares a single final route.
misconceptions.correction: Nodes flood link-state information, construct topology maps, and independently compute shortest-path trees.

misconceptions.misconception: Path-vector routing advertises only a scalar distance.
misconceptions.correction: Path-vector announcements include destination reachability and path/domain descriptions.

misconceptions.misconception: Adding a network link always improves every user’s route.
misconceptions.correction: Under selfish multi-agent route choices, Braess’s paradox shows an added road can increase travel time.

misconceptions.misconception: A full buffer is the only way to manage congestion.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes RED/WRED early drop behavior in addition to tail drop.

misconceptions.misconception: A shortest AS-level path uniquely determines the router-level path.
misconceptions.correction: Multiple router-level paths may correspond to a selected AS-level path.

misconceptions.misconception: Centralized routing is limited to a single small network.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes centralized optimization across geographically distributed private data-center WANs.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic routing prevents all routing failures.
misconceptions.correction: Dynamic routing adapts to failures, but incorrect routing, flapping, degradation, and downtime remain possible.

misconceptions.misconception: A router must inspect application payloads to choose an IP route.
misconceptions.correction: Pure IP forwarding typically uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not packet payload content.
